title: Looking After Your Eyes
paragraphs: More and more children wear glasses, and the number is growing fast.
Two things help. First, go outside for at least an hour a day. Daylight seems to protect the eyes.

title: Booking a Room
paragraphs: A photograph of a room tells you three things: the colour of the wall, the size of the bed, and nothing else.
Read the lowest recent review instead. It will tell you about the noise, the water pressure, and the walk to the bus.
Book somewhere near the station for the first night, even if it costs more.
And write down the address in the local language. You will need it in a taxi, and you will not be able to say it.

title: One Day, Three Places
paragraphs: Three places in one day is the right number, and two of them should be close together.
Morning is for the place that will be crowded. Afternoon is for the one that needs attention. Evening is for walking.
Do not plan a museum after four o clock. The legs are tired and the eyes stop taking things in.
And plan the meal. A day with no planned meal becomes an hour of argument in the street at seven.

title: Who Carries the Plan
paragraphs: Amy: I have the plan on my phone. Ben: And if your phone dies? Amy: You have it on paper.
Ben: I do not have it on paper. Amy: That is why I printed two copies. One is in your bag.
Ben: What is the first thing tomorrow? Amy: The temple at eight, before the groups arrive.
Ben: Eight? Amy: Eight. You can sleep on the train in the afternoon, which is also on the plan.

title: The Day We Stayed In
paragraphs: On the third day it rained so hard that the streets were rivers and the buses stopped.
Our plan had a mountain on it. We crossed it out and stayed in the room, playing cards and eating biscuits.
By the afternoon we were bored, and boredom turned out to be useful. We talked for three hours without a screen.
The mountain is still there. My sister and I still talk about the card game.

title: After the Trip
paragraphs: The part of a trip nobody plans is the part after it: the photographs, the receipts, and the bag you do not unpack.
Do one thing on the first evening back. Empty the bag, put the washing in, and write five lines about the trip.
The five lines are worth more than two hundred photographs you will never look at.
A trip ends twice. Once when you come home, and once when you stop talking about it. The five lines delay the second one.

title: A Week of Small Trips
paragraphs: Last spring my family did something cheap. Instead of one long trip, we did four short ones.
Each was under two hours away: a lake, an old village, a hill with a temple, and a market town.
We left after breakfast and were home for dinner. Nobody was tired, and nobody had to pack.
By the end of the month we had seen more than we would have seen in one week away, and spent less.

title: The Best Plan I Ever Made
paragraphs: The best plan I ever made was for four people and one day, and it fitted on a card.
It had three places, two meals, one bus, and a rain option. It also had the phone numbers of two people who lived there.
What made it good was not the detail. It was that everyone had read it before we left, so nobody had to ask.
A plan is not a schedule. It is a way of stopping four people from having the same argument in a street.
